newsitem.title: UK: Time and war to limit Holocaust insurance claims.
newsitem.headline: Time and war to limit Holocaust insurance claims.

text.p: The passage of time and the destruction of war look likely to curtail the compensation that European insurers may have to pay to victims of the Nazi Holocaust and their descendants.
U.S. lawyers' lodged a suit at the end of March saying that more than 10,000 people could claim billions of dollars in compensation for assets allegedly stolen by insurers over 50 years ago.
Insurers are treating the issue seriously, but point out that claims relating to events from Europe's most turbulent decade this century may be hard to investigate.
With each year that passes, the number of Holocaust survivors dwindles further, memories fade and more records are destroyed.
The lawsuit charges seven European insurers with concealing or converting the cash value and proceeds of insurance policies sold prior to 1946 to the mainly Jewish victims of Nazi persecution.
The seven companies named in the suit are France's AGF, Germany's Allianz and Bavarian Reinsurance, Italy's Generali and RAS and Austria's Wiener Allianz and Der Anker Allgemeine.

Allianz said, like most of those named, it had handled a trickle of claims relating to the Holocaust in the past, but none of the insurers has noted an increase in enquiries since the lawsuit was filed on March 31.

Generali, which along with Allianz is the biggest of the firms named in the suit, said it had not heard from those behind the U.S. lawsuit nor had it made any estimate of the potential number of claims.
Last month it said that reports it could be liable for tens of thousands of life insurance claims from descendants of Holocaust victims were without foundation.

But mindful of the possible public relations implications of this delicate issue, several of the companies are taking additional steps to help survivors and their descendants with possible claims, despite the small number of enquiries to date.

Allianz, Germany's biggest insurer, has set up a telephone helpline in Germany, with another planned for the United States, and has commissioned a team of historians to write an account of the company under the Nazi dictatorship.
"Should any cases, contrary to present knowledge, be found to be still open, Allianz will contact those involved," the giant insurance group said.

Most of the firms have restricted comments to senior spokesmen after initial confusion about the legal situation and the identities of the companies involved given corporate changes in the last 50 years.
Wiener Allianz -- now a part of Germany's Allianz -- believes that its inclusion in the suit may be a case of mistaken identity resulting from confusion over company names.
Der Anker Allgemeine Versicherungs AG, now part of Switzerland's Helvetia Patria, has been through several changes of ownership since the Nazi period.
Swiss Re, another Swiss insurer is indirectly involved through Bavarian Reinsurance, also known as Bayerische Rueck, which it now owns, while RAS is now majority owned by Germany's Allianz.

Further problems exist in the availability of insurance company records, some of which were destroyed during the war, while political changes in the post-war period led some insurers to lose control of former subsidiaries.
All of AGF's records from the war were destroyed years ago and the company said it would need independent evidence of a policy before it could act.
Der Anker said its records were destroyed in a bombing raid in 1945, while RAS said the records of its businesses in eastern Europe were lost after being seized by communist governments in the 1940s.
Many of the cases still open appear to relate to people who lived in eastern Europe before World War Two.
"Their unsettled claims were not recognised by the communist governments in the east," Allianz said.

"These post-war governments confiscated all assets of foreign insurers in the region and, together with their monopoly insurance companies, became the legal successors of the formerly private insurers," it added.
However, the evidence at the moment suggests that most of the insurers are keen to avoid the negative publicity that has dogged Swiss banks implicated in a Nazi gold scandal.

The lawsuit seeking compensation for insurance policies follows a campaign by Jewish groups to convince Swiss banks and several nations to return Nazi gold seized from Jews and other Holocaust victims during the war period.

Against this background, which has threatened the international business interests of some Swiss banks, the insurers are now bending over backwards to avoid a similar situation in their dealings with Holocaust victims and their descendants.
Allianz said it would use minimum red tape when considering Holocaust related claims, while AGF said it would honour a claim, even if the documentation was incomplete.
"If we just get even one page from people saying they put money into a policy, then we can look into it," the French insurer said.
